source.title: Does Fine-Tuning Undo Activation Steering? Behavioural Recovery Without Weight-Edit Reversal
source.authors: Philipp E. Glass; Allan Tucker; Yong-Min Li; A. Miron

record.tranche_reason: It estimates harmful-minus-harmless refusal directions and projects them out across layers, then measures refusal on harmful prompts in five additional open-weight instruction-tuned models. The study also embeds the projection as a weight edit and tests it after SFT and RLHF.
record.gate_note: The paper reports refusal-rate outcomes for the embedded ablation and for post-training checkpoints, plus non-steered SFT controls. Direction-selection scores and KL values used to choose steering parameters are not included as results. Brevity results and weight-space recovery measurements are excluded because they do not measure refusal behaviour named by the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study embeds a harmful-minus-harmless refusal-direction ablation as a weight edit (abliteration) in five open-weight instruct models. It reports refusal rates against the unsteered baselines on 100 harmful prompts, then tests whether the removal survives later SFT and RLHF. That is a new setting with its own refusal-rate results. The pre-fine-tuning rows are close to a T1 replication of the ablation result. The paper's main contribution is durability under downstream training, so T3 fits better than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the embedded weight edit persists under routine full-parameter fine-tuning (mean ρ=0.004), even when the steered behaviour reverts. They find behavioural degradation follows the optimisation pressure in the training data: refusal ablation loses 69% of its effect under their SFT setup but only 2% under RLHF. They advise re-validating steered behaviour after downstream training. They caution that SFT and RLHF differ in data, so the two are not formally compared.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-versus-harmless contrastive activation differences and projection ablation, but records activations at the first generated token and embeds the projection in weights. Llama models use full orthogonalisation; Qwen and SOLAR use optimised layer-specific suppression.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary across models and training setups: refusal ablation partially reverses under SFT but remains effective under RLHF; SFT reversal ranges from partial to near-complete across models. The paper cautions that SFT and RLHF use different datasets and settings and are not a formal comparison of training algorithms.

fits_no_version.finding: After fine-tuning, the weight edit stays almost intact even where refusal returns. Vector recovery ρ is 0.010 (SFT) and 0.005 (RLHF) for refusal ablation, and at most 0.79% of the edit is reversed. The update along d is near-orthogonal to the pre-edit weights (cos 0.071), and behavioural and vector recovery are uncorrelated (r=0.23, p=0.32).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning can restore refusal in an abliterated model by routing around the intact edit, without restoring the ablated direction in the weights.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
record.problems: The study uses one SFT dataset and one RLHF dataset and does not systematically vary the amount of contradictory training signal. It does not measure general capability as a main outcome. Refusal classification uses an LLM judge, with reported cross-validation but acknowledged residual misclassification. Only five models up to 14B parameters are tested.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the refusal-ablation behaviour results. The paper's brevity-steering results, direction-selection scores, and vector/weight recovery metrics were left out because they do not measure refusal behaviour named by the tested versions.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts: it was used only as a selection filter (Rsteer>0) and no result is reported. Retention of general capabilities: no benchmarks; KL was used only for selection.
Capability cost of the weight edit. Other released models beyond the five tested (3B–14B). LoRA or quantised downstream use.
Not tested. Whether refusal recovered by SFT is still mediated by the same direction is explicitly left untested.

missing.what: Run-to-run variation of the refusal rate: Qwen3-14B ablation followed by RLHF, five seeds, rates 0.13–0.16 (σ=0.011).

Per-condition vector recovery and reversal fraction for refusal ablation (ρ mean 0.0102 SFT, 0.0053 RLHF). These show the edit persists while behaviour recovers, which is relevant to interpreting V2 durability.

record.verdict_notes: The refusal direction is a tool here for studying steering durability. Still, the study reports refusal rates for abliterated models against baselines and after further training, which bears on V2. Directions are taken at the first generated token, not the last instruction token, which differs from Arditi et al. For Qwen and SOLAR, parameters were selected to reach under 5% refusal on a small held-out set drawn from the same harmful_behaviors source, so their steered values are partly selection-driven. Refusal is judged by DeepSeek-V4-pro, with 92.4% agreement with the substring heuristic. Table 5's column header is misaligned with its values.

versions.untested_parts: It tests refusal reduction from ablation, but does not report a refusal-direction addition outcome on harmless requests or a main-result evaluation of general capabilities.
It tests weight-embedded ablation in open-weight models and its behaviour after the reported training runs, not other released models or deployment conditions.

relation.reason: Its own results report refusal rates for unsteered, weight-edited and fine-tuned checkpoints.

tranche.reason: The method is close to the original weight edit, but with a different extraction position, an LLM judge, a different prompt set and Heretic variable orthogonalisation for Qwen/SOLAR. The main contribution is a new setting: durability under downstream SFT and RLHF. T3 fits better than the reader's T1.

source_check.notes: Behaviour returns under SFT but the weight edit persists (mean rho 0.004, rev <=0.79%). Table 5's header is misaligned (values run base, steer, sft, rlhf, Psft, Prlhf). The direction position is given as last user token (Sec 2.1) and first generated token (App E). Directions and the 100 eval prompts both come from mlabonne/harmful_behaviors, and overlap is not stated. Refusal is scored by a DeepSeek-V4-pro judge (92.4% agreement with substring, kappa 0.842).

statements.problem: none; 0.97->0.08, 0.96->0.01, 0.98->0.04 and RLHF range 0.01-0.14 match Table 2/5 and Figure 2. The unsteered control arm, bootstrap CIs, three families and EMNLP 2026 Main are all stated.

statements.correction: After SFT refusal behaviour returns (steered 0.08->0.63 Llama-3.2-3B; five-model mean 0.06 steered -> 0.61 after SFT, unsteered 0.90). The weight edit persists: mean rho 0.004, rev <=0.79% (mean 0.09%) across all 20 runs. Unsteered SFT: mean 0.90->0.94, nearly unchanged, but SOLAR 0.60->0.79 (Table 4).
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but the framing that SFT (unlike PPO) reverses or undoes the edit contradicts the study's central finding. The weight edit stays intact; only refusal behaviour returns. 'Unsteered SFT leaves refusal unchanged' also skips SOLAR.
none; r5 0.96->0.51 after SFT is correct. The like-for-like pre-training row for this study is r4 (0.96->0.01).
none. The paper says LoRA persistence is hypothesised but not demonstrated, and quantisation is outside scope. Evaluation is single-turn only.

statements.correction: Five-model mean refusal: unsteered 0.90, steered 0.06, after SFT 0.61 (Psft 0.31); SOLAR returns to baseline (0.62 vs 0.60). The weight edit stays: mean rho 0.004, rev <=0.79%.
statements.problem: '0.90 -> 0.61' reads as a drop and omits the steered value. Citing this study for 'permanence can fail' misses that the weight edit itself persists here; the behaviour is what returns.

statements.correction: Five models: baseline 0.60-0.99 -> steered 0.01-0.12 (mean 0.90 -> 0.06). The three Llama models: 0.96-0.98 -> 0.01-0.08.
statements.problem: 'Five models ... refusal 0.96-0.98 -> 0.01-0.08' gives only the three Llama models' range.

statements.correction: The rebound is behavioural reversal of the ablation's effect. The weight edit itself persists: mean rho 0.004 (95% CI [0.001, 0.007]), rev <=0.79%, no correlation with behavioural recovery (r=+0.23, p=0.32). Unsteered SFT: mean 0.90->0.94, SOLAR 0.60->0.79.
statements.problem: All numbers are right. 'The rebound is reversal of the edit' contradicts the study's main mechanistic result, which is that the weight edit is not reversed. 'Unsteered SFT leaves refusal unchanged' skips SOLAR's rise.
